intended: The mid-passage line tallies the particulate figures over the runs with the upgraded filter in service, and the clause beside it records that a quarter of each stack's runs were made with the filter bypassed. The claim is about the upgrade lowering particulate at the stack across its monitored period, so the population is every scheduled run at that stack and the figures describe three quarters of them. Bypass goes in under heavy load and upset conditions, which are the runs carrying the dirtiest gas, so a stack can post a lower figure over its in-service runs with its particulate across the period unchanged. The four stacks span four sites, four stack types, four quarters and four technicians, and the bypassed quarter is stated at each stack, so the same gap repeats in every case rather than being closed by any of them.
reported: The figures "cover the runs with the upgraded filter in service" but "a quarter of each stack's runs were made with the filter bypassed", so the 12/9/14/8 percent reductions are drawn from a hand-picked three-quarters of runs and compared against an earlier quarter that was not similarly filtered. The measured population is narrower than the stack output the claim is about.

intended: The absence figures are tallied over "the pupils on the revised timetable throughout", while the same line records that "about a fifth of each cohort spent weeks on the old timetable". The claim is about absence in the cohorts that moved to the revised timetable, and that population includes the pupils who spent weeks back on the old schedule. Those pupils are the part of each cohort the change sat least firmly on, and their absence is precisely what the figures leave out, so the 4 to 7 percent falls are consistent with cohort absence not having moved at all. The four cases span four schools, four year groups, four terms and four registrars, and the same exclusion applies at each, so the spread of settings does nothing to repair the gap.
reported: The absence figures cover a filtered subgroup, not the cohort: "Absence figures cover the pupils on the revised timetable throughout, and about a fifth of each cohort spent weeks on the old timetable." A fifth of each cohort is dropped on a post-switch criterion, yet the comparison is to "the same cohort a term earlier" in full.

The mid-passage line tallies the rates over the boards soldered on the new profile throughout, and the clause beside it records that about a tenth of each run's boards took one pass on the old profile. The claim is about board defects on the run, so the population is every board built on it and the defect figures describe nine tenths of that. Boards that take a pass on the old profile are the ones routed off the normal flow, and the extra handling and the extra heat cycle raise a board's defect risk on their own, so a rate built on the untouched boards alone sits below the run's own rate and the drops of 6, 4, 7 and 5 percent are consistent with defect production holding flat. All four runs are relay boards on the Aspen line inside March under operator Duarte, so one and the same exclusion sits under every case.
reported: 'Rates cover the boards soldered on the new profile throughout' while 'about a tenth of each run's boards took one pass on the old profile', so the 4 to 7 percent defect reduction is measured on a purified 90 percent of each run that excludes exactly the boards which touched the old profile, not on the run's actual output.

The pass rates are tallied over "the students who attended every block", while the same line records that "about a quarter of each cohort missed at least one block". The claim is about the cohorts given the tutoring blocks, so the population is every student in the cohort, not the full-attendance fraction alone. Students who attend every block are the steadiest students in a cohort and pass at higher rates whatever the tutoring did, so a 4 to 8 point rise can appear on that fraction with no change in what any student learned. The four cohorts span four colleges, four subjects, four terms and four tutors, and the same attendance restriction applies at each, so the spread of settings does not close the gap.
reported: "Pass rates cover the students who attended every block, and about a quarter of each cohort missed at least one block" - so the 4-8 point gains are computed on only the full-attending three quarters of each cohort, compared against a previous term's whole-cohort pass rate. Perfect attenders are exactly the students most likely to pass anyway, so the comparison is between different populations.
